newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to send special enovy to Cambodia.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to send special enovy to Cambodia.

text.p: Former congressman Stephen Solarz is being sent to Asia on a special mission to work with regional countries in pursuing a resolution to the Cambodia crisis, the State Department said Thursday.

Solarz will leave on Friday or Saturday for a trip to Beijing, Tokyo, Bangkok, Jakarta, Kulala Lumpur and Phnom Penh, where he will meet Hun Sen, the Cambodia leader who took power in a coup nearly two weeks ago, spokesman Nicholas Burns said.

"During high-level meetings in those capitals he will discuss with those governments how best to uphold and restore the principles of the 1991 Paris peace accords so that all Cambodian parties can operate freely and free and fair elections can take place in 1998," he said.
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright has asked Solarz "to explore possible resolution of the crisis in Cambodia," Burns added.

As Cambodia is going to dominate the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) meeting in Kuala Lumpur later this month, Albright "felt strongly that we had to have a series of diplomatic conversations with ASEAN countries as well as Hun Sen to ... make sure we had best possible framework" going into ASEAN, Burns said.

Solarz is a former long-time chairman of the House of Representatives subcommitee on Asia and the Pacific and a key player in U.S. policy leading up to the 1991 Paris treaty that brought a brief peace to Cambodia.
Burns described Solarz' appointment as a "one trip" mission not a permanent appointment.

Solarz's job would be to work with Indonesia, Thailand, the Philippines and other countries in the region on a common approach toward Cambodia, where co-prime minister Hun Sen assumed sole power after overthrowing first prime minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh nearly two weeks ago.

The United States has been pushing for Hun Sen to recreate a coalition with Ranariddh's royalist party and recommit to democratic principles including holding another round of elections as planned next year.

But while Hun Sen has given lip service to some of these democratic ideals, the United States has complained that his actual behaviour has been contradictory, including unilaterally naming a replacement for Ranariddh and threatening political opponents. A diplomatic source in Phnom Penh said on Wednesday 40 Cambodians have been killed since the coup.

Some American foreign policy experts said they detect a split in the Clinton adminsitration between officials who believe Washington should be pragmatic and work with Hun Sen and others who believe the United States should take a hardline following the coup, which unravelled a multi-billion dollar international peace effort.
Burns said Solarz' discussions would be based on the five core principles of U.S. policy toward Cambodia.

This includes: condemnation of the use of force to overturn the 1993 elections and bring about government change; support for national unity and self-deternmination for the Cambodian people; and support for the right of Cambodia's political parties to operate freely.

In addition, the United States is committed to holding free and fair elections in 1998 and is opposed to allowing senior Khmer Rouge leaders, responsible for more than one milion deaths when they ruled Cambodia in 1975-79, to play a political role in the country.
The United States said on Wednesday it was "very concerned" by a decision to make Cambodian Foreign Minister Ung Huot the country's co-prime minister and did not recognise him in that position.

The U.S. Senate voted 99-0 late on Wednesday to halt U.S. aid to Cambodia until the secretary of state certified that the Cambodian government was established by free and fair elections, and not by force or coup d'etat.
